gallery.title: File:Westminster Abbey (The Collegiate Church of St Peter) 2.jpg
gallery.description:
Westminster Abbey (The Collegiate Church of St Peter). Ten 20th-century martyrs from across the world are depicted in statues erected in 1995 above the Great West Door of Westminster Abbey. Nine heraldic shields, from reign of King George II. The abbey's two western towers were built between 1722 and 1745 by Nicholas Hawksmoor, constructed from Portland stone to an early example of a Gothic Revival design. In 1723, on the death of Wren, he became architect to Westminster Abbey, the west gable (1735) and towers (1734-1745) of which are his. Heraldry, left to right:
1: Order of the Bath. The Lady Chapel is associated with the Order of the Bath
2: Nassau? The coat of arms of the House of Nassau is prominently associated with King William III (William of Orange), who was crowned King of England, Scotland, and Ireland in Westminster Abbey in 1689
3: Kingdom of Middlesex (and of Essex)
4: Royal Arms of England 1406-1603 (possibly intended for King Henry VII (1485-1509) who built the Lady Chapel)
5: (centre) Royal arms of King George II (1727-1760) (Royal arms of Great Britain (1714-1801)). Identified as King George II because the arms of  w:Joseph Wilcocks (1673-1756)  Dean of Westminster 1731-56 (presumably when this element was built), also appear (see 6), and he served as Dean entirely during the reign of King George II
6: Coat of arms of Westminster Abbey impaling Ermine, a chief chequy azure and or, arms of w:Joseph Wilcocks (1673-1756)  Dean of Westminster 1731-56 (presumably when this element was built), Bishop of Gloucester, Bishop of Rochester (Burke, Sir Bernard, The General Armory, London, 1884, p.1110 "Wilcox alias Nowers, Leicestershire, 1732", but with chief chequy or and sable), another or and gules)
7: Coat of arms of the City of Westminster originally granted 1 October 1601 to the Borough of Westminster "Quarterly: 1st and 4th, Azure a Portcullis with chains pendant Or on a Chief of the last between two united Roses of York and Lancaster a Pale charged with the Arms of King Edward the Confessor (i.e. the old arms of the City of Westminster originally granted 1 October 1601 to Borough of Westminster, regranted by royal warrant dated 6 November 1901 to Metropolitan borough. Source: A.C. Fox-Davies, The Book of Public Arms (T. C. & E. C. Jack, London, 1915. See 25px|Westminster arms)); Now borne by the Duke of Westminster
8: Attributed arms of the Kingdom of Kent (or: Duchy of Saxony (as in the Lesser Arms of Hanover as borne by Kings of the House of Hanover (as at centre (5)))
9: A rose and thistle conjoined in a single stem (presumably signifying the union of the Kingdoms of England and Scotland)
